summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes: CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, which means identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Wider protection remains thin. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a Negative gender-identity score. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity; recourse beyond federal EEOC complaint channels is limited, and commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only.
tangentialFactors:
The Northern Mariana Islands scores as one of the weaker jurisdictions in regional comparisons. The Movement Advancement Project's data as of 27 September 2026 places its sexual orientation policy score at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy score at minus 2 of 25, with an overall score of 1.5 of 47, rated Low overall and Negative on gender identity, while marriage recognition scores full marks at 1 of 1.

The pattern across the territory's law is narrow protection rather than general coverage: enhanced sentencing for hate-motivated offences under Public Law 22-32 sits alongside an absence of comprehensive nondiscrimination protection, so a gender-identity-motivated assault can attract heavier punishment while everyday discrimination in employment, housing and services outside government employment has no commonwealth statute to fall back on, leaving federal EEOC recourse as the main avenue.

The territory's legal position on relationships is settled and liberal by regional standards, with same-sex marriage legal since 2015 and adoption available from the same year, which contrasts with the negative gender-identity score and suggests the divergence between relationship recognition and trans-specific protection that visitors may notice in how the two issues are treated publicly.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change is available to Northern Mariana Islands residents provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process; there is no self-determination route without it.

Discrimination protection at the commonwealth level extends to government employees only, beyond federal law. Private-sector residents have no commonwealth statute covering gender identity or sexual orientation and must rely on federal EEOC complaint procedures.

Hate-motivated crimes attract enhanced sentencing under CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, which sets criteria for offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity and applies within the Commonwealth Code.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry since 2015 and to adopt since 2015; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced: whether territory-issued identity documents, such as driver's licences, permit a gender-marker change independently of the federal passport process, or what evidentiary standard the specified medical process requires in practice.

Not sourced: any enforcement record for the enhanced-sentencing provisions of Public Law 22-32, including whether a gender-identity-motivated offence has been charged under it and what sentence was imposed.

Unresolved: whether the January 2025 order ending federal funding for gender-affirming care affects privately run, non-federally funded clinics in the Northern Mariana Islands, and whether any such care remains obtainable in the territory on a self-pay basis.

The Movement Advancement Project figures cited are stated as of 27 September 2026 and may not reflect subsequent legislative action; the current status of any proposed commonwealth nondiscrimination bill is unresolved in the available inventory.
